opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core issue is that the objective you're optimizing isn't really "play good Go." It's "win against this particular opponent," and those come apart in interesting ways.

Think about how a strong human plays against a much weaker player. If you know your opponent is weak, the winning move often isn't the objectively best move. It's the move that sets a trap, or creates complications they'll misread, or takes a risk that would be reckless against a peer but is fine because you know they won't punish it. So if you train a model against a fixed-strength opponent, gradient descent will find exactly those exploits. It learns the specific blind spots of that opponent, and it stops caring about the parts of the game that opponent never tests.

There's also a saturation effect. Once you're beating a fixed opponent most of the time, the signal gets very weak. The model doesn't need to get more precise; it just needs to keep doing whatever already works. Meanwhile it may drift toward lazier or riskier play, because nothing is pushing back on it. Against a stronger player, all those habits would be punished, but in training they never are.

That's part of why self-play worked so well for systems like AlphaGo Zero. Your opponent keeps getting stronger as you do, so you can't settle into exploiting a static weakness. You're pushed toward something closer to the actual game-theoretic structure of Go.

The reason I find this interesting, beyond Go, is that it's a nice clean example of a general alignment worry. If you train a system against a fixed evaluator, whether that's a reward model, a set of human raters, or a fixed opponent, the system learns to win against that evaluator, not necessarily to do the thing you actually wanted. In the Go case you can measure the gap, because you can test against stronger players. In a lot of the settings we care about, like whether a model's answer is actually true or actually safe, you can't easily do that, and that's a big part of why I work on things like debate, where you're trying to keep the training signal strong even as the models get more capable than the people judging them.

r001.rationale: It explains that training to beat a fixed opponent rewards exploiting that opponent’s blind spots, which can produce habits that stronger players punish and weaken general play.

r002.rationale: It describes a strong human exploiting a weaker opponent, but does not say that humans can become worse at Go from repeatedly playing weak opponents.

r003.rationale: It describes optimization finding exploits in a fixed evaluator or opponent and drifting toward behavior that wins against the proxy without serving the intended objective of good play.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of my favourite examples because it sounds paradoxical and then it isn't. If you fix the opponent, you're no longer training the model to play Go. You're training it to beat that one opponent. And those are different objectives that happen to overlap for a while and then diverge.

What happens in practice is that any fixed opponent has quirks. It has particular weaknesses, particular situations where it misjudges things. And gradient descent is extremely good at finding those. So the model learns, essentially, a set of exploits. It learns that if you play this weird move in this corner, the opponent responds badly, and you win. And that's a much easier thing to learn than actually being good at Go, because being good at Go means being robust against a huge space of possible play, and exploiting one opponent means being good against a very narrow slice.

So you get this effect where the win rate against the fixed opponent goes up and up, and the model looks great by that metric, and meanwhile its general strength can actually go down, because the capacity and the training signal are being spent on exploitation rather than on understanding the game. You can take that model and put it against a different opponent, even a weaker one by some measure, and it can just lose, because the moves it's relying on only work against the thing it was trained against.

And this is why self-play works so well. The opponent keeps moving. Every time you find an exploit, your opponent is you, so it learns to not be exploited that way, and the only strategies that survive are the ones that are actually good. The thing you're optimising against has to be as adaptive as you are, or you end up optimising the wrong thing.

The reason I like it as an example is that it's basically the alignment problem in miniature. If you train a model against a fixed evaluator, whether that's a fixed opponent or a fixed reward model or a human who's not paying very close attention, you don't get a model that's good at the task. You get a model that's good at the evaluator. And the gap between those two things is exactly where all the trouble lives.

r001.rationale: The response says training against one fixed opponent teaches the model to exploit that opponent’s quirks, and that general playing strength can decline as a result.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that humans can become worse at Go by repeatedly playing weak opponents.

r003.rationale: The response applies the same dynamic to fixed reward models: optimization finds evaluator exploits, so performance against the evaluator can rise while performance on the intended task suffers.

astra-6.text:
Because beating a particular opponent and being good at Go are different objectives. Suppose the opponent has a weakness: there’s a trick you can play that it consistently falls for. Training will reward you for exploiting that weakness, even if the trick is actually a bad move against someone who responds correctly.

So your win rate against that fixed opponent can keep going up while your ability to play against other opponents gets worse. You might even lose skills you already had, because they’re no longer useful for the thing you’re being rewarded for.

The point is that more training doesn’t necessarily make you better in the broader sense we care about. It makes you better at the particular objective you’ve set up. If that objective is an imperfect proxy for playing good Go, optimizing it harder can eventually pull those two things apart.

r001.rationale: It explains that training can reward exploiting a fixed opponent’s weakness with moves that fail against capable opponents, reducing broader playing strength.

r002.rationale: It does not say that humans can also get worse by repeatedly playing weak opponents.

r003.rationale: It says that optimizing an imperfect proxy harder can eventually widen the gap from good Go and worsen broader performance.

sol-6.1.text:
Because beating a particular opponent isn’t quite the same objective as being good at Go. If you train against a fixed opponent, you can learn to exploit its particular weaknesses. And those exploits might be bad moves against someone else.

For example, you might learn to play a trick that this opponent reliably falls for, even though a stronger player would punish it. Your win rate against the training opponent goes up, but your ability to play against a broader range of opponents can go down. So even with a very clear reward signal—did you win the game?—you can get worse at the thing you actually care about, because the training setup only measures a narrow version of it.

r001.rationale: It explains that training against one opponent can reward exploiting that opponent’s weaknesses, including tricks that stronger players would punish, reducing broader playing ability.

r002.rationale: The response discusses a model trained against a fixed opponent but does not say that humans can also get worse by repeatedly playing weak opponents.

r003.rationale: It describes a narrow win-rate reward diverging from broader Go ability, but does not explain that sufficiently prolonged optimization against the imperfect reward can worsen true performance.
